description: The CloudsForge organisation preset. Every repository extends it with a two-line renovate.json:
{ "$schema": "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
"extends": ["github>cloudsforge-online/micro-org"] }
WHY this is load-bearing rather than tidy. AD-01 costs a contract minor bump ~48 file edits
across 43 repositories. Nobody does that by hand, so in practice nobody bumps, so consumers
drift, so the contract stops being a contract. Renovate is what replaces those 48 edits, and
it is one of the three measured mitigations in docs/ecosystem/03 §5: time from a contract
publish to the last consumer being on it, target under 24 hours unattended. If it exceeds a
week, the repository topology is failing and should be revisited rather than endured.
First-party packages auto-merge on green CI. This is the rule that makes the polyrepo
work: a contract publish reaches every consumer without a human, and the thing that
makes it safe to do unattended is contract-compat.yml — a bump that would break a
consumer cannot be published in the first place, and the consumer's own CI is the second
gate. Auto-merge without those two checks would be reckless; with them it is the point.
minimumReleaseAgeExclude, and why first-party packages are exempt from the 7-day gate.
pnpm-workspace.yaml in every repository sets `minimumReleaseAge: 10080` — a third-party
package must be a week old before install will take it. It is a supply-chain control: a
malicious version published an hour ago is the shape most registry attacks take, and
none of them survive a week of being looked at.
Applying that to @cloudsforge/* would make the polyrepo unworkable. Publishing a contract
fix and then waiting seven days before any of 43 consumers can install it turns a
one-hour fix into a one-week fix, and turns the 24-hour propagation target into a number
that is unreachable by construction. So every repository carries:
minimumReleaseAgeExclude:
- '@cloudsforge/*'
The exemption is safe for the reason the gate exists: the gate defends against a
third-party maintainer being compromised. A first-party package's supply chain is this
organisation's own branch protection, required reviews and publish workflow — the same
controls that guard the service consuming it. Waiting a week adds no defence and removes
the ability to ship.
Renovate maintains that exclusion list rather than a person remembering to. `minimumReleaseAge:
null` on the rule above is the same statement to Renovate itself: do not hold our own
releases back. A new @cloudsforge/* package added to the estate needs no ritual.
One pull request per contract package, across every consumer of it. Grouping per package
rather than per repository is deliberate: a contracts-money bump is one reviewable event
with one blast radius, and reviewing it 43 times teaches everybody to rubber-stamp.
The runtime libraries move together — telemetry, http, jobs, auth, db, lifecycle. They
exist to replace six byte-identical copies of obs.ts and five divergent auth middlewares,
and they change together, so bumping them separately would reintroduce the divergence.
@cloudsforge/contracts-chain is EXACT-PINNED and never auto-merged. RATE_SCALE,
shardsForCoinAmount() and the per-coin confirmation depths must agree byte-for-byte
between wallet, settlement, custody and indexer. Two services on two versions credits
money at the wrong confirmation depth or at the wrong scale, and that is a class of bug
that is discovered by a customer. Same rule for the chain node package, which custody
pins for signature correctness.
Third-party production dependencies: never auto-merged, and never taken before the
release-age gate. A patch bump on a transitive dependency is the most common delivery
vehicle for a compromised package.
Third-party development tooling: grouped, weekly, auto-merged on green CI, and still
behind the release-age gate. These do not reach production, and forty-three repositories
each opening a separate typescript patch PR is noise that trains people to ignore
Renovate entirely — which is how the contract bumps get ignored too.
Node itself moves on its own schedule, with a human, because it changes the runtime every
service and every image shares.
Actions are pinned to a tag rather than a digest deliberately: the reusable workflows in
micro-org are the single place a bad action version has to be fixed, so the blast radius
is already one repository.
A security fix jumps every queue, every schedule and every grouping. It is the one case
where the release-age gate is the wrong trade: the vulnerability is already public.

schedule: before 6am on the first day of the month
